name: Humanin

lead: Humanin is a small peptide made from mitochondrial DNA, discovered in 2001 during Alzheimer research. In longevity circles it is promoted as a way to slow aging, which people connect to staying youthful-looking.

It is reported to block apoptosis by interfering with Bax and to act on cell-surface receptors including formyl peptide receptors. Laboratory and animal work links it to cell protection, insulin action and inflammation. Studies are in cells, animals and observational human work; no human trials have tested it as a treatment, and none looked at skin or visible aging.

paras: It is a research peptide discussed in longevity communities, with no established human routine.
No human safety data from treatment trials were found. Some research reports it may impair chemotherapy and promote tumor growth in cancer models. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: Humanin is promoted as a mitochondrial peptide that protects cells and could slow aging, which people tie to looking younger for longer. The research so far is in cells and animals.

lead: Humanin is a 24-amino-acid peptide encoded within mitochondrial DNA, in the gene for 16S ribosomal RNA, and was the first mitochondria-derived peptide identified [1][2]. In longevity and biohacking discussions it is grouped with MOTS-c and other mitochondrial peptides as a possible lever on how the body ages, the hope being that protecting cells from stress would show up as healthier tissue and a younger-looking body over time. These are proposals drawn from laboratory findings rather than documented cosmetic outcomes.

It was discovered in 2001 by several groups working on different questions: a Japanese team screening for factors that protect neurons from Alzheimer-related toxicity [3], and groups studying the apoptosis protein Bax [4] and IGFBP-3, a binding protein of the IGF-1 system [5]. Laboratory and animal research has since linked it to cell protection, insulin sensitivity and inflammation [6][7][8], and engineered analogs such as humanin-glycine (HNG) are widely used in experiments [1].

Humanin is not an approved drug. Human work consists of measurements of natural humanin levels, for instance after exercise or in kidney and heart patients, while studies of humanin given as a treatment in people have not been published. Some cancer-model research also reports effects that run against its protective reputation, discussed below [1].

paras: A 2001 expression screen identified a gene whose product protected neuronal cells from death caused by familial Alzheimer disease genes and amyloid-beta [3][9]. In 2003 humanin was reported to suppress apoptosis by interfering with Bax activation [4] and to bind IGFBP-3 [5]. It is also a ligand for the formyl peptide receptor family [10].

Reviews describe humanin as a mitochondrial signaling peptide, with a later-found counterpart, MOTS-c, also encoded in mitochondrial DNA [7][2][8]. Work in rodents reported a central role in regulating peripheral insulin action [2], and a 2016 study reported that mitochondrial-derived peptide levels vary with age and relate to apoptosis, insulin sensitivity and inflammatory markers [6]. A transcriptome study of major depression and suicide is also listed among humanin-related literature [11]. Some research cited on Wikipedia reports that humanin may impair chemotherapy and promote tumor growth in certain cancers [1].

The humanin gene sits inside the mitochondrial 16S rRNA gene (MT-RNR2). Wikipedia describes the peptide as folding into a short helix, and notes that the full 24-residue form is produced in the cytosol while the mitochondrion makes a slightly shorter form; both are biologically active [1]. Related copies called MTRNR2L genes occur in the nuclear genome, though whether all are expressed is unclear [1]. Seven other small humanin-like peptides (SHLP1 to SHLP6 plus humanin) are encoded by the same gene, while MOTS-c comes from the neighboring 12S rRNA gene [12].

Analogs have been engineered for research. HNG replaces one serine with glycine and is reported to be far more potent than the natural peptide in some assays, which is why it is the most used laboratory variant [1]. Shorter fragments keep some activity at lower potency [1].

Inside cells, humanin is reported to bind Bax and keep it from triggering apoptosis [4], and to bind IGFBP-3 [5]. Outside cells it acts on cell-surface receptors, including formyl peptide receptors [10] and a receptor complex involving gp130, as summarised in Wikipedia [1]. Reviews describe humanin as a mitochondrial signaling peptide, or mitokine, that conveys mitochondrial stress to other tissues [13][7][8].

A review of the IGF-1 connection reports that humanin binds IGFBP-3 and lowers circulating IGF-1, and that IGF-1 in turn influences humanin levels; its authors note that how the two regulate each other remains to be worked out [14]. Reviews of energy metabolism report that circulating mitochondria-derived peptides are lower in obesity, diabetes and aging, while muscle expression of humanin rises with mitochondrial stressors such as exercise [12].

Interest in humanin as an anti-aging molecule rests mainly on animal and cell data. Wikipedia reports that overexpression in the roundworm C. elegans extended lifespan, apparently via autophagy, and that humanin protects against oxidative stress, atherosclerotic plaque and heart-attack damage in disease models [1]. A review of mitochondria-derived peptides notes that humanin and MOTS-c improved insulin sensitivity in mouse models of type 2 diabetes, that a potent analog blocked cardiac fibrosis in aging mice, and that levels correlate inversely with growth hormone and IGF-1 expression, a pattern some researchers link to slower aging [15].

The same review adds a complication: in one report both humanin and MOTS-c amplified the inflammatory secretions of senescent cells, so the hypothesised role as a senescence-clearing agent was not confirmed [15]. A 2023 review of mitokines in aging concludes that levels shift with age and may influence age-related metabolic, cardiovascular and neurological disease, while stating that whether those changes are a cause or a consequence is still being studied [13].

Humanin is also a recurring subject in the cosmetic-anti-aging conversation because mitochondrial decline is a central theory of skin and muscle aging. No study listed here has examined humanin in skin, hair or physique.

Exercise physiologists have measured humanin directly. A review reports that acute high-intensity exercise raises humanin and MOTS-c in muscle and plasma in humans, while evidence for lasting change with training is conflicting and may depend on type, duration and intensity [16]. A randomized trial in men with impaired glucose metabolism reported that humanin protein in skeletal muscle rose after a period of resistance training [17], and a randomized crossover study found that acute endurance exercise raised circulating mitochondrial-derived peptides [18]. For readers interested in physique, this places humanin as a molecule that training appears to raise naturally, which is the basis for the 'exercise mimetic' idea attached to this peptide family.

Wikipedia summarises experimental work in which humanin impaired chemotherapy and promoted tumor growth in triple-negative breast cancer models and in glioblastoma, which sits in tension with its protective profile in other tissues [1]. These are laboratory results; the relevance to people using or considering peptides has not been studied.

Humanin is sold as a research peptide in the same online marketplace as MOTS-c and other longevity peptides, and is discussed in biohacking and longevity circles. Wikipedia notes that the related peptide MOTS-c is not approved for any condition, has been on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list since 2024, and has reportedly been injected as part of a peptide-stacking trend despite a lack of robust human data [19]. Humanin research originated in Pinchas Cohen's laboratory at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology, which also discovered MOTS-c, and in other groups [1][19].
No studies found of humanin administered to people as a treatment.

Human research to date measures the body's own humanin. A randomized exercise trial in people with mild to moderate Alzheimer disease measured humanin along with BDNF in blood vesicles of neuronal origin to track exercise effects [20]. A trial of resistance training reported higher humanin protein in muscle of men with impaired glucose metabolism [17], and a trial of acute endurance exercise reported higher circulating mitochondrial-derived peptides [18]. A 2025 randomized trial of exercise and astaxanthin in type 2 diabetes included humanin among the redox-sensitive markers examined [21]. An epigenome-wide study reported altered methylation of a humanin-like nuclear gene in large-artery atherosclerosis stroke [22].

Registered studies are observational, measuring humanin levels in acute kidney injury, cardiac surgery and renal transplantation [23][24][25]. No published trial has examined humanin or HNG for skin, hair, body composition or other aspects of appearance.
